title: Melchizedek (Genesis 14:17–20)
hook: a mysterious priest-king brings out bread and wine and blesses Abram

segments.voice: Yesterday, kikkar, the round green plain Lot chose. Your line: you choose first. Today ends the week.

Lot's green plain didn't stay peaceful. Chapter fourteen is a war story: four kings against five, armies sweeping through the Jordan valley, and Lot carried off as a captive with everything he owns. Abram hears, gathers three hundred eighteen men from his own household, chases the raiders north by night, and brings Lot back, with the people and the goods. As he comes home, two kings come out to meet him. One is the king of Sodom, who wants to make a deal. The other comes out of nowhere, says almost nothing, and vanishes from the story.
screen: `FOUR KINGS AGAINST FIVE.` → `ABRAM BRINGS LOT BACK.` → `TWO KINGS COME OUT TO MEET HIM.`

segments.voice: Here he is, in the King James Bible: "And Melchizedek king of Salem brought forth bread and wine: and he was the priest of the most high God." A king, and a priest, both at once. Salem is usually taken to be an early name for Jerusalem, and in Hebrew it sounds like shalom, peace. His own name, Malki-tsedeq, means my king is righteousness. He blesses Abram: "Blessed be Abram of the most high God, possessor of heaven and earth." And Abram gives him a tenth of everything, the first tithe in the Bible. Then Melchizedek is gone. No parents named, no birth, no death, no other appearance in Genesis. That silence made him fascinating. A psalm, the hundred and tenth, speaks of a king who is "a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek." The letter to the Hebrews, centuries later, builds a long argument on him: a priest without father, without mother, who points ahead, it says, to Jesus, a priest of a different order. And the bread and wine? Many Christians, especially Catholic and Orthodox, have seen in them an early sign of the Lord's Supper; the oldest Roman Mass prayer still names Melchizedek's offering. Others read it more simply, as a royal welcome of food for tired soldiers. Both readings start with the same scene: a stranger from no tribe the story names, blessing Abram with a meal. That ends a week of water and fresh starts: the flood, a leaf, a bow in the clouds, a tower, a call to go, a choice, and now, bread and wine and blessing.
screen: `A KING AND A PRIEST AT ONCE.` · `SALEM AND SHALOM.` · `NO BIRTH, NO DEATH, GONE.` · `A PRIEST FOREVER, IN HEBREWS.` · then, large: `HE BROUGHT FORTH BREAD AND WINE.`

segments.voice: Think of someone coming back from a battle of their own, a long shift, a hard week, and picture them walking in the door, tired. Then picture what you could put in their hands: not a feast, just bread, soup or coffee, offered with a good word. If you pray, you can ask a blessing on them.
Melchizedek. King of Salem and priest of the most high God, who meets Abram with bread and wine and a blessing, and then disappears.
Your line: bread and wine and blessing. Plain food, a good word, and then he's gone. Three hundred fifty days now.

howItsDone: Many Christians remember Melchizedek at communion: the Roman Canon of the Catholic Mass names his offering, and the letter to the Hebrews, read in many churches, calls Jesus a priest after his order.

fork.setup: you're Abram, coming home from rescuing Lot. a king you've never met comes out with bread and wine and blesses you. what do you do?

fork.reveal: "and he gave him tithes of all." Abram asks nothing, and Melchizedek vanishes from the story.
